2-1.B: Upriver is only the road away.
2-1.why: the day ends on "it turned upriver", and nothing yet says how far it went. If A, the tracks should end within a day; if B, they run on for days. Lead 1 (the steady horse that knows the lane in full dark) backs A: these people live near. B rests on the chapter: the farmer's "moving like they'd done it before" echoes the Fenmark boy "a whole county away". Lead 3 (ruts deeper coming down) backs both: they carried something away, but not where to. Lead 2 (ruts run past his gate) speaks to neither. Days 3 and 4 settle it.
2-1.weak: both are true, and the chapter already says the cart came three nights ago ("You are too late to stop it").

2-4.B: They won't change a thing for us.
2-4.why: the chapter's own question is "before they finish?", so the pace is what matters tonight. If A, expect them to move fast or move Corin; if B, there is still time. Lead 1 (the second lamp, filled and trimmed, nobody grabbed it in a hurry) and lead 3 (the chant never stopped under the shout) back B. Lead 2 (the pale scar, a stone that fell all the way down) backs A: we caught them off guard. The chapter backs both: they haul the ladder away (A), and the new ladder shows "they mean to use this place for a long time" (B).
2-4.weak: B ends the argument; either way they know.

3-1.B: Home is only the first stop.
3-1.why: it argues over the day's two open lines: "they told her she was going home first" and "Why would anyone take a stolen child back to where she was born?" If A, she'll be in or near Ashcombe; if B, the trail goes past it. Lead 1 (Corin's grey mitten, smelling of sheep) backs A: she really is going back to sheep country. Lead 2 (a cask topped up to the brim) backs B: a long road ahead. Lead 3 (Corin stood facing west, then went the cart's way) backs both. Day 2 moves it both ways: she passes within a mile of her door, then goes on up the black road.
3-1.weak: the chapter already says it: "'Somewhere warm' is home: Ashcombe."

3-2.why: same meaning, plain words, and it now mirrors B. It rests on the mother's "I've been lied to by better men than him. That wasn't what this was." The leads keep their leans: lead 2 (the made bed in the cart) A, lead 3 (sacking to quiet the hooves) B, lead 1 (the boy at the well) both.
3-2.weak: A reads awkwardly. The fork itself is strong.

4-5.A: They still move Joss by boat.
4-5.B: Joss is held in one place now.
4-5.why: it is the chapter's own question: "where did the boat take him, and what has it been doing since?" If A, follow the boat to find him; if B, the ferry is for something else, and he is in a fixed place. Lead 1 (long, unhurried curls in the boat) and lead 2 (a dry blanket folded under the stern seat) back A: he spends long nights in this boat. Lead 3 (three willow shoots cut days apart) backs B: someone fetches him wood, so he can't fetch his own. The chapter gives both: a ferry "night after night" (A); "kept eight nights… waiting for something" from Day 3 (B). Day 6 settles it.
4-5.weak: both can be true at once, so there is nothing to argue.

5-2.why: the chapter leaves this open: the dogs stop "as if they had forgotten what they came for" (A), and the one you beat "wags its tail, once, as if asking what it has done" (B). If A, expect more each dusk, aimed at us; if B, anyone on the road is at risk, like the family. Lead 3 (tracks come in together, straight from the north) backs A. Lead 2 (one clean bite on the farmer, from his own yard) backs B: they turn on anyone. Lead 1 (heads down when the beat stops) backs both. (Claude: the backup pair is used, so no reading suggests the city knows the party.)
5-2.weak: the day's summary states A as fact.

5-3.A: The bar keeps the world out.
5-3.why: it answers the chapter's own question: "Who bars a dead city from the inside, year after year?" If A, whoever keeps it will meet anyone who comes in; if B, what is inside will show itself (the standing soldiers on Day 4 and the hall's doors on Day 5 move it). Lead 3 (the stair was smashed with hammers long ago) backs A: nobody was meant to climb in. Lead 2 (the bar was put up in the last few days) backs B: shut tighter just as the heartbeat began. Lead 1 (one trodden path from the bar up to the fire) backs both. The chapter backs B too: "Something on the far side is holding them up." No new lore: it does not say who bars it.
5-3.weak: the chapter says someone keeps it shut "now", and B is an "it's a trap" option that ends the talk.

5-5.A: Their count began when the Stones drank.
5-5.B: Their count was set long ago.
5-5.why: the chapter does not say when the count began. It gives clues both ways: the watch has gone on "every night since he could stand", and the hearth is "older than anyone sitting at it" (B), but the board holds only "rows of strokes", not centuries of them (A). If A, they are answering what we did; if B, they knew this night was coming before we were born. Lead 2 (every head lifts at the beat) backs A: their watch moves with the heartbeat, which began when the Stones drank. Lead 1 (every stroke in one hand, gone over many times, never redrawn) backs B: the whole count was written out once, long ago. Lead 3 (more bedrolls than people) backs both. "Stones drank" is already known (Gathering 4; Week 5 opening).
5-5.weak: one-sided. One stroke each dusk is plainly a date, and Gathering 5 names it the next night.

6-1.A: They think the light was nothing.
6-1.B: They know someone's in the wall.
6-1.why: we're safe tonight, but what the Order believes now is open. If A, the search stops; if B, they keep hunting the wall all week. The chapter backs both: "searching by rote, they do not expect to find anything" (A), and "He saw a light. He did not see where." (B). Lead 1 (no light inside, no lantern reaches in) backs A. Lead 2 (the man with the chalk stops and looks down at the wall before he strikes) backs B. Lead 3 (old soot in a niche turned away from the slit) backs A: the room was built to hide a light. Nothing here touches the fragment's words or where anyone ran.
6-1.weak: the chapter settles it: "you are not found."

6-4.A: The rock waits for the dark moon.
6-4.B: The rock will open for us now.
6-4.why: it is the open end of the day: blank rock, and beside it "a full moon, with its whole face scored dark". If A, come back on the night; if B, find how to open it before then. Lead 2 (two foot-hollows where the soldier stood facing out a very long time) backs A: this door is about waiting. B rests on the chapter: "Every one of them has opened for you". It is backed again by tonight's fragment once it is solved ("only our blood will open"). Lead 1 (untouched grit) and lead 3 (the heartbeat is loudest at the rock) back both. Day 6 settles it ("here", and the scored moon). It never points at the other door.
6-4.weak: the chapter already says A ("the Seekers' own way in"), and B is "it's a trap".

6-5.A: The Seekers chose the dark moon.
6-5.B: The dark moon came by chance.
6-5.why: the record shows that he fell on a dark moon. It does not say why. If A, the moon is part of the lock, and the night itself matters; if B, the moon is only a date to keep. Lead 2 (slates of long sums, crossed out and begun again) backs A: someone was working a night out in advance. Lead 3 (the last rows cut in a hurry) backs B: events overtook the watchers. Lead 1 (the same spacing, year on year) backs both: anyone could know when a dark moon comes. It stays clear of the banned question: whether that night ends the waking or finishes it.
6-5.weak: low stakes, and the chapter has already counted forward ("The page and the wall agree").

1-3.text: {friend:Aim}, from his hollow in the bracken, what was he watching?
1-3.why: Straight to the fork: guarding the rock, or waiting for us. Aim = watching.

1-4.text: {friend:Charm}, when Fenmark shut its doors on us, who was it protecting?
1-4.why: The fork word for word (the girl, or itself). Quiet day: no joke.

1-5.text: {friend:Intellect}, two children, two winters apart. One man's habit, or someone's way of working?
1-5.why: The fork (same man, or a way of working), built on Garrick's own opener ("two winters between two children").

2-1.text: {friend:Aim}, the cart turned upriver. How far do you think it went?
2-1.why: Matches the new fork (kept close upriver, or only the road away).

2-3.text: {friend:Intellect}, did that stranger die trying the lock, or was he left for us?
2-3.why: The fork (same door, or a warning).

2-4.text: {friend:Charm}, the voices below all said the same words. What were they getting ready?
2-4.why: The fork here is weak (audit A2). This pushes the day's real question; canon summary: hooded figures "making something ready". Charm's notice line is the voices. No "ritual" word.

2-6.text: {friend:Might}, you've heard them digging. Cutting a way in, or searching for something?
2-6.why: The fork (to get in, or to find what's there). Might = knows digging; brings Might back to the week.

3-1.text: {friend:Intellect}, they took Wren back to where she was born. Why home, of all places?
3-1.why: The day's story already answers the fork ("somewhere warm" is Ashcombe; audit A2), so this pushes the next question instead, which leads into W3D3's fork (children chosen for the place, or places for the children).

3-2.text: {friend:Charm}, why would men taking a child bother with good manners?
3-2.why: The fork (manners are real, or the trick). Quiet day: no joke.

3-4.text: {friend:Agility}, you followed Wren's chips up the ridges. Left for us, or for herself?
3-4.why: The fork word for word. Agility = the one who climbed after them.

3-6.text: {friend:Aim}, a lamp went into the hill ahead of us. Whose was it?
3-6.why: Built on the day's callback ("a lamp went in ahead of you"); feeds the fork (go in now, or watch the lamp first).

4-1.text: {friend:Craft}, the ropes were cut clean in the dark. His own hand, or another's?
4-1.why: The fork (he had help, or didn't need any). Canon: "The ropes were cut clean."

4-4.text: {friend:Intellect}, why would Meira use an old song's word when a plain one would do?
4-4.why: Picks up Garrick's opener about Meira's gloss; the fork (just the marked children, or something else). Does not say the word itself. See doubt 1.

4-5.text: {friend:Aim}, they moved Joss by water once. Would they risk the lake again?
4-5.why: Matches the new fork (still moved by boat, or held in one place).

4-6.text: {friend:Aim}, whoever lay under the tower: did they follow us, or wait for us?
4-6.why: The fork word for word, from Garrick's opener ("someone lay under that tower"). Quiet day.

5-2.text: {friend:Might}, you stood over the cart. Did the beat call those dogs, or only madden them?
5-2.why: Matches the new fork. Might = the one who held the cart.

5-3.text: {friend:Craft}, new wood in brackets worn bright. Who keeps barring this gate?
5-3.why: From Garrick's own opener. Better than the fork here, which the audit called a null debate.

5-4.text: {friend:Aim}, did one of those helms turn, or did the dusk play tricks?
5-4.why: The fork (only standing, or one helm turned). Aim = the eye. Quiet day.

6-1.text: {friend:Aim}, an arrow under the window, pointing down. What does it want us to find?
6-1.why: The day already settles the fork ("you are not found"; audit A2). Canon: "Under the window, an arrow points down into the wall", which leads into Day 2.

6-2.text: {friend:Agility}, the dead passed us by on their way up. Called, or on guard?
6-2.why: The fork (answer a call, or guard the hall), from Garrick's opener.

6-4.text: {friend:Craft}, nobody has walked that crack before us. Why keep a soldier at it?
6-4.why: The fork (the Seekers' door, or a trap). Canon: a soldier stands in the crack's mouth.

6-5.text: {friend:Intellect}, the sky-watchers' record stops on one night. Why that night?
6-5.why: Matches the new fork (the Seekers chose the dark moon, or it came by chance).

6-6.text: {friend:Intellect}, not one of the dead turned its head. What do they know that we don't?
6-6.why: From the Intellect notice line ("They know where they are going"). Keeps them thinking without Garrick steering the door choice. See doubt 3.

1-2.text: She hasn't sat in that seat for three weeks. Your pages all reached you on the road within the same few days.
1-2.rests: D2: "Hasn't been back in three weeks"; D2: each of you was set upon on the road "within the same few days" and came away with a page

1-3.text: The man on the forest road was carrying her rubbing. The man in the bracken was watching her rock.
1-3.rests: D1 the rubbing; D3 the rubbing fits the rock, and the lookout lies watching it

1-4.text: The boy says they moved like they'd done it before. The little horse at the rock had sat out a winter or two.
1-4.rests: D4 the boy: "Like they'd done it before"; D3 the carved horse, "grey with a winter or two of weather"

1-5.text: The road, the rock, and tonight her shutters. Not one of those men has said a word.
1-5.rests: D1 "He does not say anything at all"; D3 "He does not say a word"; D5 "The same silence"

1-6.text: Meira had this shape on paper before any of you found a piece. Tonight the pieces drew it.
1-6.rests: D3 the rubbing is Meira's; D6 the map ends at the rubbing's shape

2-1.text: The mine wall put Tamsin's name first and Corin's second. Tamsin heard them say "the mill boy next".
2-1.rests: Gathering 1: "The first is Tamsin's"; D1 "The second name scratched on that wall is Corin"; D1 Tamsin's line

2-2.text: In the mine, that shape was a hole, and what sat in it was gone. Here it's cut into the mill's footing.
2-2.rests: Gathering 1: the mark "is a hole… it is gone"; D2 the wheel's footing (everyone sees it: player or a friend)

2-3.text: Corin was asked for by name. Today a lock that wouldn't open for a dead man opened for you.
2-3.rests: D2 "He asked for my boy by name"; D3 "It would not open for him… It gives at once"

2-4.text: Yesterday a branch swung on the slope with no wind. Today they knew you were at the shaft.
2-4.rests: D3 end: pebble, branch "still swinging, and no wind"; D4 "They know you are here now"

2-6.text: In the mine, you reached the mark after it was emptied. Tonight they're still digging toward the older room.
2-6.rests: Gathering 1 the empty hollow; D6 "They are digging toward the old room"

3-1.text: Corin was held a morning's walk from his own mill. Wren was told she was going home first.
3-1.rests: D1 carried down to the mill by mid-morning; D1 Corin: "they told her she was going home first"

3-2.text: Tamsin and Corin each came home with one cut palm, bound clean. Wren's taker said they'd only need her the once.
3-2.rests: Gathering 1 Tamsin's palm "bound in clean white linen"; Gathering 2 / D1 Corin "already cut", linen on his palm; D2 "they'd only need her the once"

3-3.text: At the Widow's Tooth a man lay in the bracken watching the rock. Here the riders went past this one without slowing.
3-3.rests: Week 1 D3 the lookout; D3 "The riders did not even slow"

3-4.text: Tamsin wasn't asleep; she was counting. Wren is dropping her chips, one by one, on their trail.
3-4.rests: Week 2 D1 Tamsin: "I wasn't asleep. I was counting."; D4 "She is dropping them"

3-5.text: At the mine someone took the time to bind Tamsin's hand in clean linen. Here someone folded one blanket with care, and threw the other down.
3-5.rests: Gathering 1 the linen; D5 "a blanket, folded with care, and beside it a second one, thrown down"

3-6.text: Corin said Wren's home was always warm. Tonight the map ends at a hill that breathes warm air.
3-6.rests: D1 Corin: "home was always warm"; D6 the Kiln breathes warm air through its crown

4-1.text: Every one of them you've fought has run at the first gap. Tonight one stood among you with a blade and cut only rope.
4-1.rests: Wk1 D3, Wk1 D5, Wk2 D5, Wk3 D1 "the first gap, and gone"; D1 "used it on rope"

4-2.text: The carter's coin has the king's face scraped off. Meira wrote that every record of him had been scraped clean.
4-2.rests: D2 the coin; Week 2 D5 Meira's margin: "every record of him scraped clean"

4-3.text: In Ashcombe a baby born when the moon goes out is given a chip of black glass. In Reedham every window is lit for one.
4-3.rests: Week 3 D2 Wren's mother; D3 the window (the fisherman: a lamp in every window on a dark-moon night)

4-4.text: At the ford, Tamsin's small prints stopped at the water. Today Joss's stop at the edge of deep water.
4-4.rests: Week 1 D6 "Small ones. They come down to the water's edge and stop"; D4 "where they stop… they got into a boat"

4-5.text: At the Widow's Tooth a little carved horse was left behind. Today, in their boat, a little carved hull was thrown away.
4-5.rests: Week 1 D3 the carved horse; D5 "a tiny hull… thrown away"

5-1.text: Meira looked for a fifth and never found one. Today, on the road north, somebody had cut a line out of a stone.
5-1.rests: Week 3 D3 Meira's footnote; D1 "Meira never found a fifth place"; D1 the waystone's second line "cut out, stroke by stroke"

5-2.text: On the Stillwater the birds went quiet at the first beat. Tonight the dogs came with it.
5-2.rests: D1 "the birds have stopped singing"; D2 the dogs come with the heartbeat

5-3.text: Upriver, somebody kept a hidden path clear and a dog on new iron. Here somebody keeps a new bar on an old gate.
5-3.rests: Week 2 D3 "keeping a way open", the staple "bright new iron"; D3 the bar is "new timber" in brackets "worn smooth"

5-4.text: On the road, when the beat stopped, the dogs stopped where they stood. These soldiers stopped mid-stride, and never started again.
5-4.rests: D2 "Then the beat stops. The dogs stop with it."; D4 the soldiers stand "mid-stride"

5-5.text: At Reedham they kept Joss eight nights, waiting for something. Here they strike off one night every dusk.
5-5.rests: Week 4 D3 "They are waiting for something"; D5 one stroke at each dusk

5-6.text: Every map before tonight was read out loud. Tonight it went hand to hand, and nobody heard.
5-6.rests: Weeks 1 to 4, Day 6: the way read aloud; D6 the map passed in silence, "Nobody heard"

6-1.text: At dusk you crossed the wall and nobody heard. By the end of the night a watchman was looking straight at your window.
6-1.rests: Week 5 D6 "Nothing else moves. Nobody heard." (pass or fail); Gathering 5 cliffhanger: the watchman looks "straight down the hill… at the slit window"

6-2.text: Last week you couldn't be sure a helm had turned toward you. Today one stood in your doorway and looked at the fallen stone instead.
6-2.rests: Week 5 D4 the nearest helm turned "toward you"; D2 "Its helm is turned to the fallen stone. Not to you." (Claude: canon says "Nobody is sure", so the line keeps the doubt.)

6-3.text: The soldiers are three streets nearer the hall. Round the Order's fire there are twice as many as before.
6-3.rests: D2 "three streets further up the hill"; D3 "twice as many round it as there were"

6-4.text: Upriver, a dog on a chain kept the hidden path. Today a soldier stood in the crack with its back to the hall.
6-4.rests: Week 2 D3 the dog on the chain; D4 the soldier "has its back to it. It is facing you."

6-5.text: The Order's board has counted down for generations. The sky-watchers' wall, counted forward, lands on the same night.
6-5.rests: Week 5 D5 the board, camped "for generations"; D5 counting forward, "The page and the wall agree"
